title: Signature Invariant Genealogy
description: Signature edition: every invariant carries its genealogy — who stated it, what incident or proof motivated it, and every time it caught a real bug. Invariants are living knowledge with history, not magic asserts; new engineers learn why each one exists. This is a Signature original method.
method: Invariants are registered with (author, motivation, catch history); the registry is browsable; each catch appends to the invariant's record.
usage: Register invariants at authoring; review genealogies during onboarding and incident reviews.

title: Signature Design-by-contract monitors (Eiffel)
description: Signature edition: Eiffel pioneered executable contracts: preconditions, postconditions, and class invariants checked at runtime on every call. The monitor is the contract — violations blame the right party (caller broke the precondition, or the routine broke its postcondition), turning debugging into contract arbitration.
method: Annotate routines with require/ensure and classes with invariant; the runtime checks them; violations raise contract exceptions naming the broken clause.
usage: Write contracts for module boundaries; run with monitoring in test; sample in production.

demo.code:
print('withdraw(amount) require amount > 0 and amount <= balance')
print('  ensure balance = old balance - amount')
print('contract monitor: violation blames caller or routine precisely')

title: Signature Self-healing invariant restoration
description: Signature edition: Detection is half the job: self-healing monitors restore broken invariants automatically — rebuild a corrupted cache from source, restart a wedged worker, re-queue a lost message. The monitor pairs every watched invariant with a restoration procedure, closing the loop from detection to recovery.
method: For each monitored invariant, define the restore procedure; on violation, attempt restore; escalate to humans only if restore fails.
usage: Test restore procedures like code (they're the real reliability); alert on every auto-restore so humans stay informed.

title: Signature Data-structure integrity checkers
description: Signature edition: Complex structures (trees, graphs, caches) get periodic integrity walks: a background thread verifies BST ordering, hash-table load factors, or cache coherence invariants. These monitors catch memory corruption and logic bugs that tests miss because they check the live structure, not a test fixture.
method: Write a check_structure() routine; run it periodically or on demand; log and alert on violations with a structure dump.
usage: Run integrity checks in staging always, in production sampled; make the dump actionable.

demo.code:
tree = [4, 2, 6, 1, 3, 5, 7]  # heap-ordered list
ok = all(tree[i] <= tree[2*i+1] and tree[i] <= tree[2*i+2] for i in range(3))
print('heap invariant:', 'HOLDS' if ok else 'VIOLATED')

title: Signature Invariant mining from logs
description: Signature edition: Production logs contain implicit invariants: 'every charge is followed by a receipt within 5s'. Mining logs for frequent temporal patterns surfaces the system's actual contracts — often surprising the team — which then become monitors. The logs teach you what to watch.
method: Mine frequent patterns from logs (sequence mining); present candidates to engineers; promote confirmed ones to monitors.
usage: Mine periodically; have engineers vet candidates (correlation isn't contract); promote the real ones.

demo.code:
logs = ['charge', 'receipt', 'charge', 'receipt']
print('mined pattern: charge -> receipt within 5s (support 100%)')
print('promoted to monitor')

title: Signature Graduated monitor strictness
description: Signature edition: Monitors run at different strictness per environment: pedantic in dev (every invariant checked, failures are errors), sampled in staging, and lightweight in production (only critical invariants, violations alert). Graduated strictness gets thorough checking where it's cheap and safety where it counts.
method: Tag invariants by criticality; configure strictness per environment; dev fails fast, production alerts.

specification.levels: dev pedantic / staging sampled / prod critical
specification.rule: cheap where cheap, safe where counts

usage: Tag every invariant's criticality at authoring time; review the production set quarterly.

title: Signature Watchdog and heartbeat monitors
description: Signature edition: Liveness invariants — 'the worker checks in every 30 seconds' — are monitored by watchdogs: miss N heartbeats and the monitor declares the component dead and triggers recovery. Every robust distributed system has them; they're the simplest invariant monitor that matters.
method: Components emit heartbeats; the watchdog tracks last-seen times; expiry triggers alerts or automatic restart/failover.
usage: Set timeouts from measured heartbeat jitter; make recovery automatic for stateless components.

demo.code:
import time
last_beat = time.time() - 45  # seconds ago
print('last heartbeat 45s ago (timeout 30s) -> WATCHDOG: declare dead, failover')

title: Signature Daikon dynamic invariant detection
description: Signature edition: Daikon watches program executions and reports likely invariants — 'x > y at this point', 'this list is sorted' — inferred from actual runs. Teams use detected invariants as monitor candidates and as documentation of what the code actually does (vs what anyone remembers).
method: Instrument the program; run the test suite; Daikon infers invariants at program points; engineers promote the true ones to permanent monitors.
usage: Run on the test suite; review inferred invariants (some are coincidental); promote real ones to asserts.

demo.code:
print('Daikon observed 500 runs of sort():')
print('  inferred: output is sorted; output is permutation of input')
print('  promoted to permanent monitors')

title: Signature Statistical invariant monitors
description: Signature edition: Some invariants are statistical — 'p99 latency under 200ms', 'error rate below 0.1%'. Statistical monitors track distributions over sliding windows and alert when the invariant breaks with significance, distinguishing real drift from noise.
method: Define the metric and window; compute the statistic continuously; alert when it crosses the threshold with significance (not on single samples).
usage: Set thresholds from baselines; require significance before paging; tune windows to the metric's natural timescale.

demo.code:
lat = [120, 130, 125, 400, 128]  # ms
p99 = sorted(lat)[int(0.99 * len(lat))]
print(f'p99 latency {p99}ms:', 'INVARIANT VIOLATED' if p99 > 200 else 'holds')
